newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Swiss merger to create bancassurance giant.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Swiss merger to create bancassurance giant.

text.p: Two of Switzerland's top financial concerns, bank Credit Suisse Group and insurer Winterthur Group, said on Monday they would merge to form one of the world's leading providers of hybrid bancassurance services.
The two blue chips said the merger was voluntary but they had hurried to avoid the prospect of a Winterthur takeover by Swiss investment banker and shareholder activist Martin Ebner.

The merger, which needs approval from shareholders and regulators, would make CS Group the biggest Swiss bank and the world's third largest asset manager for private and institutional investors, with $465 billion under management.

Lukas Muehlemann, CS Group chief executive, also told a news conference the new group would be one of the world's 10 biggest financial services companies with a stock market capitalisation of some $37 billion.
"The merger is a powerful, forward-looking response to developments in the financial services market," said Muehlemann, who will also be chief executive of the combined group.

The merger illustrates the blurring distinction between banks and insurance companies as competition heats up to offer customers one source for a wide range of financial services, often dubbed bancassurance.

Executives said the merger grew out of 18 months of cooperation in three joint ventures. But they said they had hurried after Ebner started building up a Winterthur stake now at 25 percent, plus about five percent held by Ebner customers.
"The massive arrival of a large shareholder in Winterthur posed an uncertainty to the long-term evolution of the cooperation," Winterthur chairman Peter Spaelti told a joint news conference.
Spaelti also said the merger announcement was moved up three days to Monday because Ebner's BZ Group at the weekend said it was seeking over 50 percent of Winterthur.
"The letter from the BZ Group opened the door for speculation. We wanted to provide clarity for all parties concerned," CS Group chairman Rainer Gut said.

Stock market reaction to the plan was mixed. CS Group and Winterthur shares jumped at first to all-time highs but cooled off in late morning and ended lower. CS Group was down 3.50 Swiss francs to 205 and Winterthur gave up 18 francs to 1,497.
Traders said some sellers were unhappy about CS Group's planned capital increase and short-term profit dilution.
CS Group will increase capital by 1.5 billion Swiss francs nominal value, watering down earnings per share by around four percent in 1998 before recovering, Muehlemann said.
Shareholders of both companies will be asked to approve the deal on September 5. If approved, CS Group will offer 7.3 registered shares for each one of Winterthur's.

Based on Friday's closing share prices, the swap equals a payment of 1,522 Swiss francs per Winterthur share, a premium of seven francs on the Friday close and seven percent over the average price for the previous 30 trading days.
Winterthur will then become an operationally and organisationally separate division of the Credit Suisse Group, boosting total assets to around 700 billion Swiss francs.

The combination of Credit Suisse, currently Switzerland's second largest bank, with Winterthur, the third largest insurer, should result in synergies of 300 to 350 million Swiss francs within three years from higher income and cost-cutting.
A maximum of 500 jobs worldwide will be lost, but the companies said there would be no layoffs.
Some analysts said the merger was likely to put pressure on CS Group's rivals Union Bank of Switzerland and Swiss Bank Corp to make similar moves.
"The general trend in Europe clearly goes towards bancassurance," said Thomas Della Putta of Geneva private bank Pictet & Cie.
